issues.description: The manuscript contains a direct, unresolved contradiction about when the reduction methods are administered relative to the misinformation (collaborative recall). The Introduction states the warning is placed AFTER collaborative recall, a later passage states the methods are placed BEFORE collaborative recall, and the Procedure clearly places all three interventions in Phase 3, i.e., after the collaborative recall (Phase 2) but before the individual test (Phase 4). This is not a trivial wording slip: the entire theoretical rationale for 'Demonstration and motivation' rests on inoculation theory (McGuire, 1964), which requires exposure to the protective manipulation BEFORE the persuasive attack. If the intervention actually occurs after misinformation, it is a post-warning, not an inoculation, invalidating the stated mechanism. The reader cannot determine which design will actually be used.
issues.quote: What is important, we decided to place the methods inducing resistance to misinformation before the collaborative recall phase (that is, before exposing participants to misinformation). The main reason for that is that we wanted to inoculate participants against the influence of misinformation before it could take effect.

issues.subcategory: confound between item and condition (failed counterbalancing)
issues.description: The Design section claims discussed and non-discussed items will be 'fully counterbalanced,' but the Procedure states that every pair discusses the SAME fixed set of four critical details. Fixing which items are discussed across all participants completely confounds the discussed/non-discussed (misinformation) factor with specific item content and difficulty. Any difference in accuracy between discussed and non-discussed items could be attributable to the particular items chosen rather than to the discussion/misinformation manipulation. This contradicts the explicit counterbalancing claim and undermines the central within-subjects comparison.
issues.quote: In order to ensure sufficient discussion, each pair will discuss the same set of four critical details during the collaborative recall phase. For example, all pairs will talk about Eric’s cap color and his company logo.

issues.description: Participants work in pairs that mutually exchange misinformation during the collaborative recall and are assigned to condition as a pair. The two members of a dyad are therefore statistically non-independent, yet the power analysis, sample-size statement (240 'participants'), and planned ANOVAs appear to treat all participants as independent observations. Ignoring dyadic clustering inflates the effective degrees of freedom and Type I error rate and overstates power. A multilevel/mixed model or analysis at the dyad level is required, and the power analysis should account for the intraclass correlation.
issues.quote: Considering the accessible financial, organizational and time resources, a sample of 240 participants was assumed; this allows for excellent power to detect medium and large effect sizes but not small ones.

issues.description: The Procedure specifies the individual memory test as '20 open-ended questions,' and four scoring indices (correct, misinformation-consistent, other, total) are derived from an open-ended format. However, the Analysis plan states the individual memory test 'will also use the two-alternative forced-choice format.' These are mutually exclusive response formats with different scoring logics (e.g., the 'other answers' category is only possible with open-ended responses). This contradiction makes the primary outcome measure and its analysis indeterminate and unreproducible.
issues.quote: In the present research, the individual memory test will also use the two-alternative forced-choice format.

issues.description: Only the four discussed critical details are queried during the collaborative recognition test; the four non-discussed critical details are not. Discussed items therefore receive additional retrieval practice/re-exposure relative to non-discussed items, in addition to receiving misinformation. The discussed vs. non-discussed contrast thus confounds the misinformation manipulation with a testing/retrieval-practice effect, so any accuracy difference cannot be cleanly attributed to memory conformity.
issues.quote: The test will comprise 12 questions, four of which refer to critical details (e.g., What color was Eric’s cap?), with the other eight being control questions.

issues.subcategory: effect-size synthesis from two highly heterogeneous studies
issues.description: The replication power analysis pools only two studies with extremely discrepant effect sizes (Hedges' g = 1.92 vs. 0.38) into a single random-effects estimate of 1.13. With only two studies, between-study variance cannot be estimated reliably, and the pooled estimate is unstable. Notably, the more methodologically similar study (Kękuś et al., 2020; Polish sample, modified MORI) yielded the much smaller g = 0.38; if the true effect is closer to this value, the claimed sufficient power (N=18) is a substantial overestimate.
issues.quote: Given the rather large difference in effect sizes between both studies, random effects were assumed while calculating the joint effect size, which was 1.13. This amounts to a Cohen f of about 0.57.

issues.subcategory: implausibly low repeated-measures correlation drives power
issues.description: The power analyses rely on an assumed correlation of r = 0.07 between the repeated measures (discussed vs. non-discussed accuracy). This value is unusually low for two measures from the same individuals and strongly influences the required sample size in within-between ANOVA. The provenance ('joint correlation... in both studies') and appropriateness of this single low value are not justified, and a sensitivity analysis across plausible correlation values is not reported.
issues.quote: A correlation r = 0.07 between repeated measures was assumed based on the research described above (Ito et al., 2019; Kękuś et al., 2020).

issues.description: The conditions are not matched for active engagement or duration. The 'Demonstration and motivation' condition involves an active DRM word-list task, written recall, feedback, and a motivational podcast, whereas the warning and education conditions are ~7-minute passive podcasts, and the control is an unrelated soft-skills podcast. Differences in task activity, cognitive engagement, time-on-task, and retention interval before the individual test are confounded with the content of the interventions, making any between-group differences difficult to attribute to the intended mechanisms.
issues.quote: In the control group, participants will listen to a podcast concerning soft skills related to social attitudes.

issues.description: The analysis plan states all discussed items will be categorized as containing misinformation, but the manuscript elsewhere acknowledges that a partner may have provided an answer consistent with what the participant saw (e.g., through guessing) or said 'don't know.' Categorizing every discussed item as 'misinformation' regardless of what the partner actually said is internally inconsistent with the manuscript's own scoring caveat and misclassifies the exposure, biasing the estimate of the conformity effect.
issues.quote: we will categorize all discussed items as having contained misinformation, as the collaborative recall procedure is designed to expose participants to their partner’s differing version of events.

issues.description: The authors assume directional (one-tailed) significance tests, yet they repeatedly acknowledge that some interventions (especially Education about memory, and even the demonstration) could plausibly INCREASE memory conformity by reducing confidence in one's own memory. Using one-tailed tests when the effect could credibly go in either direction is inappropriate and would fail to detect (and could misrepresent) a harmful reverse effect.
issues.quote: Comparisons among all groups and directional significance tests are assumed.

issues.subcategory: mechanism mismatch between DRM demonstration and memory conformity
issues.description: The 'Demonstration' relies on the DRM paradigm, which produces internally generated false memories from semantic association, a mechanism distinct from socially transmitted misinformation/memory conformity (source/normative/informational influence). It is not established that demonstrating susceptibility to DRM-type false memories transfers to resistance against co-witness misinformation; the assumed generalization is a conceptual leap that is not justified.
issues.quote: The demonstration of the fallibility of memory will be done by means of the DRM technique (see detailed description below); the motivational aspect will be achieved by a podcast

issues.subcategory: moderation hypothesis without a measurement/analysis plan
issues.description: A central theoretical claim is that the methods will be effective only (or more) for participants who are AWARE of the discrepancy between their own memory and the partner's information (informational influence). However, the analysis plan provides no procedure to measure awareness of discrepancies or to formally test this moderation, so the key theoretical prediction cannot actually be evaluated by the proposed design.
issues.quote: Thus, we expect that effectiveness of our methods will be higher among people aware of discrepancies between the original information and misinformation than among those unaware of such discrepancies.

issues.description: Four indices (correct, misinformation-consistent, other, total answers) will each be analyzed by ANOVA, plus average accuracy across filler/discussed/non-discussed questions, and follow-up pairwise comparisons. No correction for multiple comparisons or family-wise error control is described, inflating Type I error across the multiple tests.
issues.quote: We will explore the individual memory test’s scores for the critical details using analysis of variance (ANOVA), using all four indices: the number of correct answers, number of answers consistent with misinformation, other answers, and the overall number of answers.

issues.description: Subjective confidence ratings (0–100%) are collected for every answer, but no analysis plan, hypothesis, or role for these data is specified. Given the manuscript's heavy theoretical emphasis on confidence in one's own memory as the driver of informational influence, the absence of a confidence-analysis plan is a notable omission and risks undisclosed flexibility (researcher degrees of freedom).
issues.quote: Moreover, for each question, the participants will be asked to rate the subjective certainty of each answer on a scale from 0% (complete uncertainty, guessing) to 100% (absolute certainty).

issues.subcategory: low number of critical items reduces reliability
issues.description: Only four discussed and four non-discussed critical items per participant form the basis of the key within-subjects comparison. Such a small number of items yields low measurement reliability and unstable per-condition accuracy estimates, increasing measurement error and limiting the sensitivity of the design to detect the moderate-sized reduction effects the study targets.
issues.quote: the individual memory test ... will contain 20 open-ended questions, eight of which will cover all the critical details included in the movie, regardless of whether they were subsequently discussed.

issues.description: The authors acknowledge substantial content overlap among the three interventions (e.g., teaching about memory appears in both Education and Demonstration; warning-type content appears across conditions). This overlap makes it difficult to attribute any observed effects to the distinct hypothesized mechanisms and weakens the ability to compare the relative efficacy of the methods, which is a stated aim.
issues.quote: Secondly, we are aware of some overlap between the three interventions, for instance, teaching about memory is included is present in a way in both Education about memory and Demonstration and motivation.

issues.subcategory: weak basis for predicted efficacy ordering
issues.description: The specific predicted ranking (Demonstration and motivation > Extended warning > Education about memory) is justified largely by analogy to a single persuasion study (Sagarin et al., 2002) in an advertising context, with no direct empirical basis in the memory-conformity domain. This ordering hypothesis is largely speculative and may bias the directional tests and interpretation.
issues.quote: the Extended warning against misinformation is expected to be slightly less effective than Demonstration and motivation but more effective than Education about memory.

issues.subcategory: potential breach of MORI deception / demand characteristics
issues.description: The MORI paradigm depends on participants not realizing they viewed different movie versions. The Extended warning explicitly tells participants the partner saw a different version, and the visual-acuity cover story plus end-of-study questioning about the 'real purpose' introduces demand characteristics. Differential disclosure of the deception across conditions (only the warning condition reveals the dual-movie manipulation) is itself a between-group confound and a potential validity threat.
issues.quote: Extended warning, informing that the partner actually saw a different version of the movie and informing why the deception was applied, should make the participants who are aware of discrepancies discard the consistency assumption

issues.subcategory: ethical/consent issues for minors and broad age range
issues.description: The eligible age range is 16–35, which includes minors (16–17) in many jurisdictions, yet no mention is made of parental/guardian consent or ethics approval procedures for minors. Additionally, the wide age range is justified only by avoiding age-mismatched pairs, without describing how pairing by age will actually be controlled in assignment.
issues.quote: The participants enrolled in the study will be 16–35 years old; they will be invited to participate via advertisements in the media and on the internet.

issues.subcategory: underpowered for small effects given uncertainty
issues.description: Because no prior data exist for the novel reduction methods, the true effect size is unknown, yet the sample of 240 is explicitly powered only for medium-to-large interaction effects. Reduction-of-suggestibility manipulations frequently produce small effects; if the real effect is small, the study is substantially underpowered and a null result would be uninterpretable. This risk is acknowledged but not mitigated.
issues.quote: a sample of 240 participants was assumed; this allows for excellent power to detect medium and large effect sizes but not small ones.

issues.description: When a pair cannot agree during collaborative recall, 'both responses will be documented,' but it is not specified how such items are subsequently coded for misinformation exposure or excluded/included in analysis. This ambiguity affects the central operationalization of whether a participant was actually exposed to misinformation on a given item.
issues.quote: If the participants are unable to reach an agreement, both responses will be documented.
